summary: Gives the profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 2, which behaves like TCP's congestion control. It suits senders that want to take advantage of available bandwidth in rapidly changing conditions and can cope with the abrupt window changes typical of TCP's additive increase, multiplicative decrease. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: CCID 2 gives DCCP a TCP-like way to control sending rates when the network is congested. It counts packets, reduces its sending window after congestion, and also adjusts how often the receiver sends acknowledgements.

questions: how does dccp tcp-like congestion control work
what is ack ratio in dccp
subtitle: TCP-like congestion control for DCCP data and acknowledgement packets.

tldr.problem: DCCP needs a congestion-control profile for senders that want available bandwidth and can tolerate changes in sending rate.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 2 adapts SACK-based TCP congestion control to DCCP packets, uses Ack Vectors to track delivery, and adjusts acknowledgement frequency with Ack Ratio.
tldr.outcome: The sender cuts its congestion window when it detects loss or congestion, but DCCP does not retransmit lost data. RFC 4341 is updated by RFC 8311.

today: RFC 4341 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2006 and is updated by RFC 8311.

sections.title: What CCID 2 Is For
sections.content:
Congestion Control Identifier 2 (CCID 2) is a DCCP profile that uses a close variant of TCP congestion control with selective acknowledgement information. It suits applications that want to use available bandwidth and can tolerate abrupt rate changes when congestion occurs.

Unlike TCP, DCCP does not retransmit packets. CCID 2 counts congestion windows in packets, and it applies congestion control to acknowledgement traffic as well as data.
sections.plainLanguage: CCID 2 controls DCCP sending rates in a way similar to TCP. Lost data is not sent again, and the profile also manages the rate of acknowledgements.

sections.title: When to Use TCP-Like Control
sections.content:
CCID 2 is intended for flows that want as much bandwidth as possible over time and can tolerate the congestion window being cut sharply. Applications that prefer to avoid abrupt rate changes may use the alternative CCID 3 profile.

CCID 2 uses DCCP Ack Vectors rather than TCP SACK options to report packet delivery. Its congestion-control parameters use packets rather than bytes because DCCP is a datagram protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: CCID 2 suits applications that can handle a sudden reduction in sending rate. Applications that need smoother rate changes may prefer a different congestion-control profile.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use Ack Vectors
sections.content:
CCID 2 requires Ack Vector support on a half-connection. During connection establishment, the sender must send Change R(Send Ack Vector, 1) to the receiver.

The sender should wait for the matching Confirm L(Send Ack Vector, 1) before sending data, except that it may send data in DCCP-Request packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Before regular data transfer, the sender asks the receiver to provide Ack Vectors. The sender should wait for confirmation that the receiver supports them.

sections.title: Controlling the Data Sending Rate
sections.content:
The sender tracks the congestion window cwnd, slow-start threshold ssthresh, and outstanding packet estimate pipe. These values are measured in packets. The sender may send a data packet only when pipe is below cwnd.

A newly acknowledged packet or an inferred loss reduces pipe. After a congestion event, cwnd is halved but never below one packet. Slow start increases cwnd, while congestion avoidance grows it more gradually; a new connection starts with a window of at most four packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender counts packets in the network and sends only while it has room in its congestion window. When it detects loss or a congestion mark, it reduces that window and later increases it gradually.

sections.title: Acknowledgement Rate and Feedback
sections.content:
Each required acknowledgement carries an Ack Vector that reports which packets arrived and whether they were ECN-marked. Ack Ratio controls how often the receiver sends acknowledgements; the default value is two.

When acknowledgement packets are lost or marked, the sender increases Ack Ratio, reducing the acknowledgement rate. It lowers the ratio gradually after congestion-free windows. An active sender should acknowledge the receiver's Ack Vectors at least once per congestion window.
sections.plainLanguage: Ack Vectors tell the sender which packets arrived. Ack Ratio controls how many data packets the receiver covers with each acknowledgement, and changes when acknowledgement traffic shows congestion.

sections.title: ECN and DCCP Features
sections.content:
CCID 2 supports Explicit Congestion Notification. The receiver reports congestion marks in Ack Vectors, and returns ECN Nonce information so the sender can check whether marks were concealed.

The relevant DCCP mechanisms include the Ack Vector option and the ECN Capable, Ack Ratio, and Send Ack Vector features.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can mark packets to report congestion instead of dropping them. The receiver reports those marks so the sender can reduce its sending rate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations for DCCP and TCP congestion control. An attacker may impair a connection by dropping packets or forging duplicate acknowledgements or acknowledgements for new data.

The authors state that they are not aware of new security considerations introduced by this TCP-like congestion-control profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Forged acknowledgements or dropped packets can affect congestion control. The RFC reports no additional security issue specific to CCID 2.
